records.value:

a) explain the meaning of energy, work and power in relation to machines,
b) demonstrate the transformation of mechanical energy using simple apparatus,
c) describe applications of simple machines in making work easier,

records.old:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) distinguish between kinetic energy and potential energy and calculate each in everyday situations,
b) apply the principle of conservation of energy to explain energy transformations such as in a roller coaster or pendulum,
c) define work and calculate work done by a force, including positive and negative work and work done against friction,
d) define power and calculate it for everyday activities such as climbing stairs or lifting water,
e) explain how simple machines (pulleys, levers, ramps) reduce effort, and determine their mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency,
f) appreciate the application of energy, work, power and machines in day-to-day life.

As written, one pulley fixed above the well would only change the direction of the pull: the effort stays 200 N (velocity ratio 1). Lesson 8 and the Final Explanation (Part 4d) say exactly this, and the numbers used throughout (125 N effort over 16 m rope, MA 1.6, VR 2) belong to a fixed plus a movable pulley with 2 rope sections. The anchor story is kept; only the description of the pulley now matches the data. Check: ideal effort = 200 N / 2 = 100 N; measured 125 N gives MA = 200/125 = 1.6 and efficiency = 1.6/2 = 80%. Teachers should confirm that this matches how wells in their area are really rigged.

records.new: When the same bucket is hung from a two-pulley system (a rope over a fixed pulley above the well and under a movable pulley on the bucket), she lifts it with less effort, and a child can even do it.
records.group_headline: Phenomenon described a single fixed pulley making lifting much easier, which is not physically true; now a two-pulley system, matching the numbers used in every lesson

records.why: Expected observation was not realistic. A 0.2 kg pencil case sliding about 1 m against about 1 N of friction transfers about 1 J, which warms the block and floor by far less than 0.01 degrees C, so learners would feel nothing and might conclude the energy 'vanished'. Rubbing palms (about 10 W for 10 s, roughly 100 J spread over a small area) is felt easily. The teacher moves already use hand rubbing; the learner text now agrees. Heating by friction follows Q = energy transferred divided by (mass x specific heat).
records.old: Learners touch the plank/floor and the block after repeated slides and note warmth and any sound.
records.new: Learners rub their palms together hard for 10 seconds and feel the warmth (this is friction heating), then slide the block firmly along the rough floor several times and listen for the sound. Any warming of the block or floor is far too small to feel, so say so: the warmth in their hands is the model for where the block's energy went.
records.group_headline: Observations of 'warm blocks and sacks' after a few slides are not realistic with school equipment (the temperature rise is far too small to feel); learners now use hand rubbing as the felt evidence
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics 2e, ch. 7 Work, Energy, and Energy Resources (conservation of energy and friction); ch. 5 Further Applications of Newton's Laws: Friction, Drag, and Elasticity

records.why: A compact bucket falling freely through air loses very little energy to the air: drag is about 0.5 x 1.2 kg/m3 x 1 x 0.07 m2 x (11 m/s)2 = about 5 N at the end, so over 8 m it takes only about 15 J, not 390 J. The 390 J (11 m/s) is believable if the bucket runs down on its rope and the rope rubs in the pulley. The data stay the same; only the setting is stated so the numbers are physically reasonable and agree with the later pulley-friction story.

records.why: Lesson 3 says the speed formula is 'not derived today' and Lesson 4 lists v = sqrt(2gh) as a skill, but nowhere is it shown. Added a short worked derivation before it is used. Checked: 2 x 10 x 8 = 160, sqrt(160) = 12.65 (12.6 m/s as in the lessons); 2 x 10 x 0.5 = 10, sqrt(10) = 3.16 (3.2 m/s, as in the Explain phase).
records.old: Challenge fast groups: 'Calculate the speed the bucket would have if all 1600 J became KE, and show it equals 12.6 m/s.'
records.new: Show the whole class once how the ideal speed is found: PE = KE gives mgh = 1/2 mv squared, the mass cancels, so v = square root of (2gh) = square root of (2 x 10 x 8) = square root of 160 = 12.6 m/s. Challenge fast groups: 'Use the same idea for a 2 kg block falling 0.5 m.' (v = square root of 10 = 3.2 m/s.)

records.why: The Pendulum Lab has no 'starting height' control: it uses string length and release angle. Check: cos 37 degrees = 0.799, so 1 - 0.799 = 0.201, giving a rise of about 0.2 m as the lesson's 1 J example needs. Teachers should check what the offline copy of the simulation displays.
records.old: They set the mass to 0.5 kg and the starting height equivalent to 0.2 m, release the bob, and watch the PE, KE and total energy bars with friction set to NONE.
records.new: They set the mass to 0.5 kg, the string length to 1.0 m and the release angle to about 37 degrees (this raises the bob by 1.0 x (1 - cos 37 degrees) = 0.2 m), release the bob, and watch the PE, KE and total energy bars with friction set to NONE (read the values if the bars show them; otherwise compare bar heights).
records.group_headline: Pendulum Lab cannot be set by 'height'; learners now set length and angle to get the 0.2 m rise, and the 0.98 J versus 1 J difference is explained correctly
records.reference: PhET Interactive Simulations (University of Colorado Boulder), Pendulum Lab

records.new: If a group reads about 0.98 J instead of 1 J, say: 'Why might the numbers differ slightly? Is that a real change or a reading issue?' (The simulation uses g = 9.8 N/kg, our class uses 10 N/kg: 0.5 x 9.8 x 0.2 = 0.98 J. The total is still constant.)
records.reference: PhET Interactive Simulations (University of Colorado Boulder), Pendulum Lab

records.why: The old wording said negative work 'stores' energy, which mixes up two ideas. Correct relation for gravity: work done by gravity = minus (change in PE) = -1600 J when PE rises by 1600 J; woman's +1600 J + gravity's -1600 J = 0 J net, so KE is unchanged. Rechecked with the numbers in the lesson.
records.old: Guide: the woman transfers energy into the bucket (+1600 J) while gravity's negative work shows the energy being stored as PE. Use the phrase: 'Positive work gives energy to an object; negative work takes energy from it or stores it as the force opposes the motion.'
records.new: Guide: the woman's +1600 J of work is the energy she transfers to the bucket, and it ends up as the bucket's PE. Gravity's -1600 J is the same change seen from gravity's side (change in PE = minus the work done by gravity), so the two cancel in the net work and the speed does not change. Use the phrase: 'Positive work gives energy to an object; negative work takes energy away from it.'
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, ch. 7 Work and Kinetic Energy and ch. 8 Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy

records.why: The Sankey diagram said 2000 J of chemical energy went in. Her muscles do 2000 J of work, but the body must use about four times that much chemical energy because human muscle is about 25 percent efficient (2000 J / 0.25 = about 8000 J). The simplified sentence would leave learners with a wrong energy account for the person. The unit still treats 2000 J as the work input, so no numbers elsewhere change.
records.old: 2000 J from chemical energy in Mwende's body (from ugali and githeri) -> 1600 J PE of the bucket + 400 J heat (and a little sound) from friction in the pulleys and rope.
records.new: 2000 J of work done by Mwende's muscles (using chemical energy from ugali and githeri; muscles are only about one quarter efficient, so her body uses roughly four times this amount in total and the rest warms her body, which we do not count here) -> 1600 J PE of the bucket + 400 J heat (and a little sound) from friction in the pulleys and rope.
records.group_headline: Energy input was written as '2000 J of chemical energy' although a person's muscles are only about 25% efficient; now '2000 J of work done by the muscles', with the extra body heat noted
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics 2e, ch. 7 Work, Energy, and Energy Resources, section 7.7 Work, Energy, and Power in Humans

records.why: Teachers had no expected values for the model lift and no substitute if spring balances are missing (guidelines 8 and 13). Expected values are the classroom version of the Kitui numbers: ideal effort = 20 N / 2 rope sections = 10 N, plus friction and the weight of the movable pulley gives about 11-14 N; rope moves 2 x 0.4 m = 0.8 m; work in = 12 N x 0.8 m = about 9.6 J against 8 J gained.
records.old: Remind groups to keep the lifting speed steady and read the balance while moving.
records.new: Remind groups to keep the lifting speed steady and read the balance while moving. Expected readings: about 20 N over 0.4 m by hand (8 J), and about 11 to 14 N over 0.8 m with the two-pulley set-up (about 9 to 11 J), never below 10 N. If spring balances are scarce, hang a plastic cup on the free end of the string and add sand or water (water measured in a measuring cylinder, 1 mL = 1 g) until the load rises slowly at steady speed; effort in newtons = mass in kg x 10.

records.why: The Final Explanation never told learners to use their Summary Tables (guideline 7) and offered only writing as a way to answer (guideline 12). One short sentence now covers both.
records.old: Write your answers in the space under each prompt.
records.new: Use your Summary Tables from Lessons 1 to 8 to help you. Write your answers in the space under each prompt; if writing is hard for you, you may add a labelled diagram or explain part of your answer aloud to your teacher.

records.why: The contract allows three rubric level fields; the printed headings are fixed. The level names Exceeds / Meets / Approaches Expectations now appear at the start of each descriptor so they read correctly under any heading. Wording of the descriptors is otherwise unchanged.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: all calculations (PE, work, power, KE, MA, VR, efficiency) are correct, use g = 10 N/kg, show every step and give correct units.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: most calculations are correct with steps; one or two small slips in units or arithmetic.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: several calculations are missing, incorrect or have no units or working.

value.criterion: Explaining why the pulley feels easier
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly states a smaller force (125 N vs 200 N) over a longer distance (16 m vs 8 m) and that the work needed is not reduced.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: states the smaller force and longer distance but is unclear about the work.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: says the pulley makes lifting easier without describing force and distance, or claims the pulley reduces work or gives energy.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: identifies the chemical energy from food as the source, accounts for 2000 J = 1600 J PE + 400 J heat, and states that energy is conserved and not destroyed.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: identifies the energy source and the 400 J as heat, but conservation is incompletely stated.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: does not identify the source, or says the energy is lost or destroyed.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: correctly defines and calculates MA, VR and efficiency, and compares the machines and the fixed pulley accurately.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: calculates most of MA, VR and efficiency correctly with minor errors in comparison.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: confuses MA, VR and efficiency or cannot calculate them.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: the explanation is organised, uses scientific terms accurately and refers to the Kitui well data throughout.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: the explanation is mostly clear with some terms used loosely.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: the explanation is disorganised or uses few scientific terms.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the current partner contract only has three level fields in the Final Explanation rubric, so the Below Expectations level cannot be represented. Suggested: ask the partner whether a fourth level field can be added; until then teachers can treat anything under the 'Approaches Expectations' description as Below Expectations.
